newsitem.title: MALI: Randgold plans sharp rise in Mali gold mine output.
newsitem.headline: Randgold plans sharp rise in Mali gold mine output.

text.p: South Africa's Randgold Resources aims to raise output at the Syama gold mine in Mali to 200,000 ounces a year from 125,000 by bringing in new machining methods and boosting staff morale, a senior company official said.

"We are known for our rehabilitation strategies for mines in difficulty. SOMISY (Societe Miniere de Syama) has enormous potential, if it has not matched expectations it is because it has not been given the attention it needs," Randgold Resource's chief executive Mark Bristow told Reuters in an interview.
The exploration and new business arm of Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd took control of BHP Minerals Mali from Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP) on September 3.

The deal, which includes a 65 percent stake in the Syama mine and BHP's exploration interests in Mali, was worth $30 million cash, a $23 million loan claim and a $31 million loan to be retained by BHP and paid back over six years.
Mali's government holds 20 percent of Syama's operating firm SOMISY and the International Finance Corp has 15 percent.
Syama is one of West Africa's biggest gold mines. Its estimated resources amount to 110 tonnes of gold at an in situ grade of 4.1 grams/tonne.
BHP put its stake on the market after problems with mining deeper ores, the introduction of import duties on equipment by Mali and staff stoppages.
Raising worker productivity by giving them a bigger role in decision-making was central to management plans, Bristow said, but he did not give a timeframe for the planned production increase.
Alan Miskirin, general manager of BHP Minerals Mali, said the sale was a strategic withdrawal because Syama did not fit with BHP's policy of working large-scale projects.

"Our activities in Mali do not fit with these strategic standards. That is why we have decided to concentrate our efforts somewhere outside here, taking account of project standards which we are better able to manage," he told Reuters in an interview.
But he said BHP could retain some interest in the mine under the sale terms with Randgold.
"It is possible, notably in the case of discoveries of new deposits, that we will still be present, perhaps not physically, but as shareholders," he said.
He said BHP had created Mali's first modern industrial mine at Syama, investing $130 million and employing 500 staff. Production started in 1990.
Miskirin said the firm's partnership with Mali's government, the first Mali had signed with a multinational company, had been an "apprenticeship" for both parties.

"We have been victims of several criticisms, tied in my view to a lack of communication. In Africa, people think of mines as money, and nothing but money, but forget the work that has to go in beforehand to get this gold and this money," he said.
BHP said the sale of BHP Minerals Mali Inc to Randgold Resources was at A$45 million ($36 million) below book value and this would be reflected in its August quarter results.

One Malian government official told Reuters there was a risk that Mali would consider the sale void on the grounds that BHP had not given sufficient prior notice of the sale and had not been given the go-ahead under the terms of its partnership with the state.
